## What this tracks
This dataset measures how bicycle-friendly major roads are throughout Tennessee, rating each road segment with letter grades from A to F.

## Why it matters to you
If you're planning a bike commute or recreational ride in Tennessee, this data tells you which roads are safest and most comfortable for cycling before you head out. A road with an "A" rating likely has bike lanes and lower traffic, while an "F" rating means heavy traffic with no bike infrastructure. Business owners near highly-rated bike routes can better understand their potential cycling customer base and plan bike-friendly amenities accordingly.

## How to read this data
**RTE_NME** — The actual road name, like "CLINCH AVE." **SPD_LMT** — Posted speed limit in mph, with sample values like 45 mph. **AB_BA_OVERALL_BLOS_SCORE** — The combined bicycle safety rating for both directions of travel, ranging from A (best) to F (worst), with sample values like "B". **THRU_LANES** — Number of through traffic lanes, with sample values like 4 lanes, which affects how stressful the road feels for cyclists.

## Where this leaves you  
This dataset doesn't let you look anything up by your address, but it's still a window into how the state operates. Read it to understand the scope of the program and what the official records contain; the state's own interactive map (linked on this page) shows the locations involved.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the structural condition of every bridge in Tennessee as of 2022, based on official field inspections.

## Why it matters to you
If you regularly drive across bridges in Tennessee, this data tells you which ones are in poor condition and may face weight restrictions or closures. Business owners who rely on freight transportation can identify potential route disruptions before they impact deliveries. Residents can also see how old their local bridges are and whether Tennessee is maintaining critical infrastructure in their area.

## How to read this data
**COUNTY** — The Tennessee county where the bridge is located, like "Anderson" or other county names. **ROUTE_NUMBER** — The specific road or highway number where the bridge carries traffic, such as "02444." **OVERALL_CONDITION** — The bridge's current structural status rated as "Good," "Fair," or "Poor" based on federal inspection standards. **YEAR_BUILT** — When the bridge was originally constructed, with sample bridges dating back to 1985, and **AGE** — how many years old the bridge is as of the 2022 reporting year.

## Try it yourself
Search for your Tennessee county name to see all bridges in your area and their conditions. If you have a regular commute route, look up that specific route number to check whether any bridges along your path are rated as "Poor" and might face future restrictions.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the locations and specifications of concrete barrier walls installed along Tennessee's interstates, state routes, and major highways.

## Why it matters to you
If you're planning a road trip or daily commute in Tennessee, this data shows you where concrete barriers create lane restrictions or affect visibility on major routes. Construction companies bidding on highway projects can identify existing barrier locations to plan around. Emergency responders can use this information to understand access limitations when responding to highway incidents, since concrete barriers affect where vehicles can cross medians or exit roadways safely.

## How to read this data
**ROUTE** — identifies the specific highway, like I0040 for Interstate 40. **COUNTY_NAME** — shows which Tennessee county contains each barrier section, such as Shelby County. **FEAT_DESC** — describes the barrier type, with samples showing "Jersery Barrier" (likely Jersey Barrier, a common concrete divider design). **LOC_DESC** — indicates whether barriers are on the "Right" side or other positions relative to traffic direction. **HEIGHT** — measures barrier height in feet, with the sample showing 2.9 feet. **BEG_LOG** and **END_LOG** — mark the start and end points along the route using mile markers, like 0.141 to 0.152 mile markers.

## Try it yourself
Look up your regular highway route using the **ROUTE** field to see where concrete barriers might affect your drive. If you frequently travel Interstate 40 through Shelby County, you can find the exact mile markers where barriers are installed and plan lane changes accordingly before reaching those sections.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the locations and details of access control fences installed along Tennessee's interstates, state routes, and major highways.

## Why it matters to you
If you're planning development near a highway or need to understand property access restrictions, this data shows exactly where fencing blocks access to major roads. Property owners and developers can check whether existing or planned access points to their land might be restricted by state-installed fencing. Business owners considering locations near highways can verify whether customers and deliveries can easily reach their property from nearby roads.

## How to read this data
**ROUTE** — the highway designation where the fence is located, like "I0040" for Interstate 40. **COUNTY_NAME** — which Tennessee county contains this fence section, such as "Dickson." **LOC_DESC** — which side of the road the fence is on, showing values like "Right." **BEG_LOG** and **END_LOG** — the starting and ending mile markers where each fence section begins and ends, measured in decimal miles like 0.007 to 0.021.

## Try it yourself
Search for your county name in the COUNTY_NAME field to see all access control fencing in your area, then look up specific routes you travel regularly to understand where highway access is restricted along your commute or business routes.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the locations and details of curb and gutter installations along Tennessee's major roads, including interstates, state routes, and locally-maintained highways.

## Why it matters to you
If you're planning construction, landscaping, or utility work near a major road in Tennessee, this data tells you exactly where curb and gutter infrastructure exists that could affect your project. Property developers can identify which road segments already have proper drainage infrastructure when evaluating sites. The data also helps residents understand why certain road sections handle stormwater better than others during heavy rains.

## How to read this data
**COUNTY_NAME** — The Tennessee county where the curb and gutter segment is located, such as "Lawrence." **ROUTE** — The specific road number like "05694" that identifies which highway or state route contains this infrastructure. **BEG_LOG** and **END_LOG** — The starting and ending mile markers (like 0.01 to 0.057) that pinpoint exactly where along the route this curb and gutter section begins and ends. **LOC_DESC** — Whether the curb and gutter is on the "Right" or left side of the road as you travel in the increasing mile marker direction.

## Try it yourself
Look up your county name in the dataset to see which state routes and highways near you have curb and gutter infrastructure. If you live near a numbered state route, search for that route number to see exactly which mile segments have curb and gutter installations versus sections that might only have ditches or no formal drainage.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the locations of entrance pipes installed along Tennessee's interstates, state routes, and other major highways.

## Why it matters to you
If you're a contractor, utility company, or engineer working on projects near Tennessee highways, this data tells you exactly where entrance pipes are located before you start digging or construction. For property owners adjacent to state routes, knowing the diameter and precise location of these drainage features helps you understand how stormwater flows from the roadway and could affect your land. This information prevents costly accidents and helps you plan landscaping or development projects that won't interfere with state highway infrastructure.

## How to read this data
**ROUTE** — identifies the specific highway where the pipe is located, like "I0075" for Interstate 75. **COUNTY_NAME** — shows which Tennessee county contains the pipe, such as "Hamilton." **DIAMETER** — measures the pipe size in inches, with sample values like 30 inches. **LOC_DESC** — indicates whether the pipe is on the "Right" or left side of the roadway when traveling in the direction of increasing mile markers.

## Try it yourself
Search for your county name in the COUNTY_NAME field to see all entrance pipes along state highways in your area, then filter by the specific route number if you need information about pipes near a particular interstate or state route that runs through your property or business location.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the location and specifications of guardrails and cable barriers installed along Tennessee's interstates, state routes, and other major highways.

## Why it matters to you
If you're planning a road trip or daily commute in Tennessee, this data shows which highway segments have safety barriers that could affect visibility, emergency stopping areas, or roadside access. The data also helps you understand why certain highway sections feel safer or more enclosed than others.

## How to read this data
**COUNTY_NAME** — the Tennessee county where each guardrail segment is located, like Lawrence or Davidson. **ROUTE** — the specific highway number where the barrier is installed, such as route 05694. **FEAT_DESC** — the type of barrier system, with values like "W-Beam" for standard metal guardrails or cable rail systems. **LOC_DESC** — which side of the road the barrier protects, showing values like "Right" for the right shoulder or median areas. **BEG_LOG** and **END_LOG** — the precise mile markers where each guardrail section starts and ends, such as from mile 1.417 to 1.432.

## Try it yourself
Look up your regular highway route by searching for the route number in the **ROUTE** field, then check the **COUNTY_NAME** to find guardrail locations in your area. You can see exactly which mile markers have barriers and whether they're on the right or left side of the road, helping you identify the safest areas to pull over in an emergency.

## What this tracks
This dataset records the precise location and address information for every property in Tennessee that can receive emergency services through the 911 system.

## Why it matters to you
When you call 911, dispatchers use this data to send help to your exact location, even if you can't clearly communicate your address. If your property isn't in this database or has incorrect information, emergency responders might be delayed reaching you during a crisis. For Tennessee businesses, this data helps verify that your location is properly registered for emergency services and can help you understand how your address appears in official county records.

## How to read this data
**Add_Number** — the street number of the address, like 930. **St_Name** — the street name without directional indicators, such as "TUCKER BEND." **St_PosTyp** — the street type that comes after the name, like "RD" for road. **County** — which Tennessee county the address is located in, such as "GILES." **Inc_Muni** — whether the address is within city limits or shows "Unincorporated" for rural areas. **Zip_Code** — the postal code, like 38477.

## Try it yourself
Search for your street name in the St_Name field to see all addresses on your road and verify your property is included in Tennessee's emergency services database. You can also filter by your county name to see how addresses are officially formatted in your area.

## What this tracks
This dataset maps every road centerline across Tennessee with precise address ranges and geographic boundaries for the state's Next Generation 911 emergency response system.

## Why it matters to you
When you call 911 in Tennessee, this data helps dispatchers locate you instantly and send help to the right address. The dataset ensures emergency responders know exactly which county, city, and zip code jurisdiction covers your location, preventing delays when seconds count. It also helps delivery services, GPS navigation, and mail carriers find addresses accurately throughout the state.

## How to read this data
**NAME** — the street name like "MERIDIAN" without prefixes or suffixes. **TYPE** — the road type such as "DR" for Drive, "ST" for Street, or "RD" for Road. **R_F_ADD** and **R_T_ADD** — the address range on the right side of the street (like 600 to 698), telling you what house numbers exist on each block. **COUNTY_L** and **COUNTY_R** — which county covers the left and right sides of the street, like "WARREN" county, important since emergency services are organized by county boundaries.

## Try it yourself
Search for your street name in the NAME field to see how your road is officially mapped in Tennessee's 911 system. Check the address ranges (R_F_ADD, R_T_ADD, L_F_ADD, L_T_ADD) to confirm your house number falls within the recorded range, and verify that your county (COUNTY_L or COUNTY_R) matches what you expect for emergency service coverage.
